profiles.meeting_scenario: A design review meeting at a health-law nonprofit that is preparing a proposed editorial policy and author-guidance package for its new legal-medical scholarship journal, The Journal of Health Evidence & Policy. The team is reviewing a near-final policy draft on what kinds of literature reviews the journal will accept and how those submissions should be evaluated, prompted by recurring disputes over whether doctrinally informed narrative reviews in health law are being unfairly treated as methodologically inferior to PRISMA-style systematic reviews. The agenda is to assess whether the draft reviewer rubric, submission template, and explanatory note are ready for circulation to the editorial board. The expected outcome is a decision on whether the package is 'board-ready' and what light revisions should be made before sending it out.

members.name: Dana Feldman
members.expertise: Health law publishing standards, editorial policy drafting, legal scholarship review criteria
members.background: Former managing editor at a peer-reviewed health law journal who now leads policy and submissions design for a nonprofit publisher focused on interdisciplinary legal scholarship.
members.private_state: Wants the package approved quickly so the journal can open its call for papers on schedule, while quietly preserving broad room for expert-led, interpretive review articles that legal academics will actually submit.
hidden_assumptions: A review can be called 'systematic' if its method for selecting and interpreting authorities is transparent and justified, even if it is not exhaustive in the biomedical-review sense.
The 'board packet' is the concise decision document and rubric, not the full operational annexes that staff will use after approval.
If the draft is 'ready for circulation,' it only needs to be conceptually stable enough for board discussion rather than fully citation-clean and implementation-complete.

The examples section can cite flagship public-health commissions and legal synthesis pieces as paradigmatic 'narrative reviews' without needing to distinguish sharply among hermeneutic, critical, and integrative methods.

members.name: Arjun Mehta
members.expertise: Research integrity, publication governance, auditability, policy-risk review
members.background: Attorney with prior experience advising academic medical centers on evidence review protocols, conflict-of-interest controls, and defensible review procedures for policy-facing publications.
members.private_state: Wants to avoid a policy that could later be criticized as lowering methodological standards, and quietly aims to ensure the board sees a package that is operationally auditable if challenged by external reviewers.
hidden_assumptions: A 'systematic' review denotes a pre-specified, reproducible search-and-selection workflow that another team could materially replicate.
The 'board packet' includes all appendices needed to show how the policy will actually be implemented, including reviewer instructions and conflict-screening mechanics.
A draft is 'ready for circulation' only when the board could approve it without needing substantive operational clarification afterward.
The examples section should anchor itself in review types with recognized methodological standards, and broad expert overviews are risky to present as acceptable models unless tightly categorized.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both discuss whether the policy should allow 'systematic' methods alongside narrative reviews.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means 'systematic' in the broad sense of transparent, reasoned, and methodically described synthesis, including interpretive legal-health reviews that justify source selection without exhaustive searching.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means a pre-specified, reproducible, audit-friendly search/screen/appraisal process closer to biomedical systematic review conventions.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In interdisciplinary publishing discussions, using 'systematic' as a general compliment to rigor is common, so both hear reassuringly familiar language and assume the other shares their sense of methodological seriousness.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree they want the package 'board-ready' by Friday.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 believes 'board-ready' means the editorial principles, rubric structure, and headline examples are stable enough for discussion and provisional approval, with technical appendices to be polished later.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 believes 'board-ready' means the board could adopt the package as drafted, including implementation details, appendix references, and risk controls, without further substantive build-out.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Design review meetings often use readiness language as shorthand, and both participants are used to iterative drafting, so the phrase sounds aligned while hiding different thresholds for completeness.

misalignment_points.topic: What is included in the 'board packet'
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both refer to revising 'the board packet' before circulation.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is talking about the 8-page memo, the reviewer rubric, and the one-page author note that the board will actually read at this stage.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is including the appendices on reviewer calibration, conflict disclosures for invited expert reviewers, and the sample decision tree for classifying review types.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Each person's version is plausible in legal-policy settings: some boards see only a high-level packet while others expect supporting appendices, so saying 'board packet' feels perfectly ordinary and does not trigger clarification.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both mention using the 'commission-style review example' to illustrate acceptable narrative synthesis.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking of a multidisciplinary Lancet-style commission that synthesizes evidence and expert judgment to guide broad policy questions.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of a formal law-reform commission report with defined consultation procedures, publication protocols, and institutional accountability.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In legal and policy publishing, 'commission' naturally evokes authoritative expert work for both speakers, and each assumes the other's preferred example carries the same procedural implications.

turns.inner_thought: I need this approved without reopening the whole philosophy of review articles. If we can keep the draft framed around transparent method, then doctrinal and policy-synthesis pieces still have a home. For me, board-ready by Friday means the memo, rubric, and author note are stable enough for the board discussion; the operational cleanup can happen afterward.
turns.utterance: Thanks for making the time. I want to use this as a final check on the draft package for how the journal handles systematic and narrative reviews before it goes to the editorial board. My hope is that we can confirm it's board-ready by Friday with just a light round of tightening.

turns.inner_thought: What matters is that the board packet can stand up if anyone later asks how this policy is actually applied. Board-ready by Friday should mean they could approve the full package without us coming back to fill in basic implementation mechanics. And when I say board packet, I'm including the appendices that show reviewer instructions, conflict handling, and classification logic.
turns.utterance: That works for me. What I mainly want to confirm is that the board packet is board-ready and that the review categories will be defensible if they're questioned later.

turns.inner_thought: The key is not letting 'narrative' become shorthand for second-class. We need systematic, narrative, and hybrid interpretive reviews all recognized as legitimate so long as authors explain how they chose authorities and how they are reasoning across them. That broader sense of systematic is exactly what legal-health scholars will understand and submit into.
turns.utterance: Right. The central design choice in the draft is that we recognize systematic, narrative, and hybrid interpretive reviews, so long as the method is transparent. That gives reviewers a structure without forcing every submission into one model.

turns.inner_thought: I can live with multiple categories, but the language around systematic has to preserve a real standard. If reviewers don't see pre-specification and reproducibility as part of that category, we'll invite drift and then have no answer when someone asks why one article got called systematic and another didn't.
turns.utterance: I agree with that in principle. I do think the language on systematic reviews should preserve reproducibility and pre-specification, just so reviewers know what standard they're applying.

turns.inner_thought: The examples are how we keep this practical and reassure the board that we are not talking about loose essayism. Pair a conventional evidence synthesis with a commission-style review example—something like a big multidisciplinary public-health synthesis where expert judgment is part of the value—and the point lands without overdefining every subgenre.
turns.utterance: I think the examples section already does a lot of that work. It pairs a conventional evidence synthesis with a commission-style review example that uses expert judgment for broader policy questions, which helps show the range of acceptable narrative synthesis.

turns.inner_thought: Yes, the commission-style review example is useful because it suggests a formal process, institutional structure, and a methodology someone can point to later. If the note nods to that defined methodology, the example won't read like an open invitation to free-form expert overviews.
turns.utterance: I found the commission-style review example helpful for exactly that reason. It signals formality and process, especially if the accompanying note gestures to a defined methodology.

turns.inner_thought: Good, then we should avoid bogging this down. I can make light edits to the memo and examples, send the board packet Friday, and let staff finish the longer supporting annexes after circulation. The board does not need to wade through every implementation detail now.
turns.utterance: Then my instinct is that we're talking about light revisions before Friday. Once the board packet is circulated, staff can finish the supporting material after the meeting.

turns.inner_thought: That sounds fine as long as the packet they see already includes enough on calibration and conflicts to approve the policy responsibly. Those mechanics are part of the board packet in my mind; otherwise the board is being asked to bless a framework without seeing how risk is controlled.
turns.utterance: That sounds workable. I would just want the board packet to make the reviewer calibration and conflict-screening logic clear enough for approval.

turns.inner_thought: I can sharpen the memo so the board stops equating narrative with unsystematic. The phrasing should make clear that these pieces are differently systematic for legal-policy questions, without boxing us into a narrow biomedical template that will scare off serious legal scholars.
turns.utterance: Yes, I can tighten the memo language so the board sees that narrative reviews are not unsystematic, just differently systematic for legal-policy questions.

turns.inner_thought: As long as the materials draw a line between acceptable synthesis and unsupported expert say-so, I'm comfortable. The packet should show that reviewers have a basis to distinguish grounded narrative work from ad hoc opinion, and ideally that logic is visible wherever the board looks.
turns.utterance: That makes sense. I'm comfortable so long as the distinction between acceptable narrative synthesis and ad hoc expert opinion remains clear in the packet.

turns.inner_thought: Great. I'll revise the memo, adjust the examples, keep the commission-style review example in place, and send the concise board packet Friday afternoon. If Arjun wants to look at the larger support materials later, fine, but I don't want that to slow circulation.
turns.utterance: Perfect. I'll take the final edits on the examples and the memo, and I'll send the board-ready packet Friday afternoon.

turns.inner_thought: Once I see the revised packet, I'll do a last legal-risk pass and make sure the appendices and controls are solid enough for circulation. The overall architecture is good; I just need confidence that what's going out as the board packet is complete in the operational sense.
turns.utterance: Sounds good. Once I see the revised packet, I'll do a quick legal-risk pass, but the structure looks solid for circulation.
